body:
Found by hunting for regressions the #1657 forward fix could introduce — in the
guard I added to prevent one.

## The guard

cps/editbooks.py `upload_book_formats` and cps/tasks/convert.py `TaskConvert`
both refuse to split a KEPUB when the book already carries any annotation.
Rationale: splitting renames spine documents, a Kobo matches Bookmark rows by
ContentID, so renaming strands every existing highlight.

That is correct for the case it was written for — a book that has been in the
library unsplit, has been read and highlighted, and is now being re-uploaded or
re-converted.

## Where it inverts

MEASURED 2026-08-19: the splitter's piece naming is DETERMINISTIC. Splitting the
same source twice from scratch produces byte-identical member names — verified on
Nineteen Eighty-Four, 25 split members, two independent runs, identical lists
(`OEBPS/part0003_split_000-split-1.xhtml`, `-2`, `-3`, ...).

So consider a book BORN SPLIT once #1750 ships:

  1. the book is created split; its chapters live in `X-split-1.xhtml`,
     `X-split-2.xhtml`, ...
  2. the reader highlights a chapter; the device stores a ContentID naming
     `X-split-2.xhtml`;
  3. the user re-uploads the original, unsplit KEPUB for that book.

The guard sees annotations and withholds the split, so the stored file has the
ORIGINAL single-document layout. `X-split-2.xhtml` no longer exists in the
package and the highlight is stranded — which is exactly what the guard exists
to prevent.

Had it split, the deterministic naming would have reproduced `X-split-2.xhtml`
and the highlight would have survived. **For this case the guard causes the harm
it was written to avoid.**

## Why it is still net-positive today

Case A (never split, annotated) is every book that exists right now, because
nothing has ever been born split. Case B cannot arise until #1750 ships and a
user annotates a book created after it. So the guard is right for the whole
current population and wrong only for a population that does not yet exist.

That is a reason to fix it before that population appears, not a reason to
ignore it.

## Fix direction, and why I did not just ship it

The distinguishing question is whether the CURRENTLY STORED package is already
split by us. If it is, re-splitting the replacement reproduces the same names and
is the anchor-preserving action; if it is not, the guard's original reasoning
holds.

Two reasons that is not a two-line change:

* `upload_book_formats` writes the uploaded file over the stored one BEFORE
  normalization runs (`requested_file.save(saved_filename)`), so the old package
  has to be inspected before the save or the evidence is gone.
* "already split" has to be detected without lying. The piece-name pattern our
  splitter produces (`<stem>-split-<n>.<ext>`) is a marker, but a package could
  carry such names from another tool, and a replacement upload could be a
  different EDITION whose split would produce different names anyway — in which
  case the anchors are lost regardless of what we do.

Getting the detection wrong re-introduces case A harm, which is worse and
affects every existing book. So it needs the device experiment behind F-3e383a
(does a Kobo re-download at all?) to be settled first, otherwise we would be
optimising the delivery of a file the device may never fetch.

## What is pinned meanwhile

A test asserts the CURRENT behaviour — an annotated book's upload is not split —
so the choice is visible and deliberate rather than accidental, and this finding
is what it points at.
title: The do-not-split-annotated-books guard inverts for a book that was born split
